Primary Word Stress. Although primary word stress is not predictable in Guayabero — the syllable bearing primary word stress can occur word initially, medially, or finally with no cooccurrence restrictions — it always occurs on either the ultimate or penultimate syllable of the grammatical stem, thereby identifying the stem in speech. Furthermore, syllable-final consonant clusters occur only in stem-final syllables bearing primary stress, so the maximum expansion of a syllable is always associated with primary stress. new_statements.quote: 3. Acento. El estado fonémico del acento se establece por los siguientes contrastes: /pasá/ 'pantano' /pása/ 'llegar' ... /nehéla/ 'nuevo' /nehelá/ 'su pelo (de usted)' /ámo/ 'tú deberías decir' /amá/ 'aquí está' ... /asá/ 'otro' /ǽsa/ 'anzuelo' [fn. 2:] En términos generales la anexión no afecta el acento. Los autores suspendieron sus investigaciones antes de poder definir las bases para el cambio en la acentuación cuando ocurre. ... [p. 54:] La palabra fonológica se compone de una a cinco sílabas. Se marca con pausa posible, aumento de velocidad prenuclear, y un núcleo caracterizado por acento primario y tono alto simultáneo: /ben/ 'casabe' /mɨ́ntat/ 'en el agua' /pihimélisdoʔ/ 'de nuevo'
new_statements.translation: 3. Stress. The phonemic status of stress is established by the following contrasts: /pasá/ 'swamp' /pása/ 'to arrive' ... /nehéla/ 'new' /nehelá/ 'your hair' /ámo/ 'you should say' /amá/ 'here it is' ... /asá/ 'other' /ǽsa/ 'fish-hook'. [fn. 2:] In general terms affixation does not affect the stress. The authors suspended their research before they could define the basis for the change in stress placement when it occurs. ... [p. 54, 4.2:] The phonological word consists of one to five syllables. It is marked by potential pause, prenuclear increase in tempo, and a nucleus characterised by primary stress and simultaneous high pitch: /ben/ 'cassava bread' /mɨ́ntat/ 'in the water' /pihimélisdoʔ/ 'again'.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog record (Keels 1985: contrastive, not predictable): Waller & Waller establish stress as phonemic with minimal pairs on di- and trisyllables (pasa/pasa, nehela/nehela, amo/ama, asa/aesa) and write it in the orthography as an acute. They state no window and no default position; compatible detail added: the phonological word (1-5 syllables) has one nucleus with primary stress and simultaneous high pitch, affixation ('anexion') generally does not move the stress, and stress conditions segmental allophony (theta for /d/ after stressed vocoids, lax [open o] in unstressed syllables). One of their phonological-word examples, /pihimelisdo?/ 'de nuevo', carries the primary stre…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is phonemic (lexically contrastive): minimal pairs differ only in stress position, on disyllables and trisyllables, so its position is not predictable and it is written with an acute accent in the practical orthography. Each phonological word (1-5 syllables) has one primary-stressed nucleus, realised with simultaneous high pitch; affixation generally leaves the stress in place (unexplained exceptions noted). No fixed position, window or weight condition is stated.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing stated (only one primary-stress nucleus per phonological word is described; phrase-level pitch patterns are treated separately in 4.3).
new_statements.exceptions: Footnote 2 (p. 52): affixation generally does not affect stress, but some stress shifts under affixation occur whose conditioning the authors could not determine before suspending fieldwork ('nuevos estudios.. seran publicadas en fecha proxima').
new_statements.identity_note: Guayabero (jiw), Guahiboan, spoken on the Guaviare river (Meta/Guaviare, Colombia); Tobar Ortiz 2000 maps the settlements Cano Ceiba, Barrancon, La Sal, Barranco Colorado, Mucuare, Laguna Barajas and notes an older vs younger speakers' pronunciation difference. Waller & Waller 1976 and Kondo 1998 are SIL-Colombia (Lomalinda) descriptions of the same language; no dialect split is at issue.

sources.quote: 'A pesar de que el acento primario de palabra no es predecible en guayabero -- la silaba que posee acento primario puede ocurrir al comienzo de la palabra, en el medio de esta, o al final, y no hay restricciones co-ocurrentes -- siempre se presenta, o bien en la ultima silaba, o en la penultima de la raiz gramatical, identificando en esta forma la raiz.' (Spanish original says 'raiz' = root where the 1985 English says 'grammatical stem'.)

sources.quote: No rule for stress placement is stated. The orthography section only notes that diphthongs 'por lo general se acentuan en la primera vocal' and that ph/th are aspirated 'en posicion inicial de una silaba acentuada'; headwords carry a written acute accent whose position varies lexically (buya 'flecha', jela vs. athi 'sainos', jalwek 'buscar', kaka 'oso perezoso', to'a 'mandar'), consistent with unpredictable stress within a final two-syllable window but not an explicit statement.
